subject: N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?

messages.author: b03783d2b6589c68
messages.subject: N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
parts:
Greetings to all,


I have a question regarding the suitability of N-mixture models for our analysis of the relative abundance of prey species in the landscape, and I was hoping for the forum’s candid opinion/comments/suggestions.


Background:

Together with colleagues, we are analysing ungulate count data from road surveys in a large landscape in Africa, with the intent of examining how medium/large herbivores influence lion resource selection.

The data on the prey species was obtained during single-visit surveys of roads, where we counted tracks. From the number of tracks traversing the road, we estimated the number of individuals detected in each spatial replicate (2km road segments). There is no difference in the road substrate – it is all sand, and tracks are typically easy to see. We have ~475 sites (i.e. 64 km2 square grids) with typically three to seven 2-km segments within each cell (spatial survey replicates).

Since we are not interested in specific species’ relative abundance, we have lumped detections of lion prey species in three categories/”species” - small/medium/buffalo. “Downgrading” our data to 0/1 detection – non-detection, we saw that there is clear evidence of heterogeneity in detection probability of prey due to abundance variation among sites (as expected Royle-Nichols models performed much better than MacKenzie models). Also, thankfully, there was no evidence that there is need to consider Hines models of spatial-correlation in detection of prey in the adjacent road segments (i.e. the 2km segments were sufficient large). This analysis was run in Presence stand-alone software because of the need to consider Hines models as well.


Question:

We plan to use N-mixture (pcount) models for our analysis from now on, to make most of the data in hand – i.e. the counts. We understand that we are not interpreting N to mean abundance but a relative abundance across our sites. However, we are concerned by the fact that our ungulate species that we have lumped together in small/medium/large species detection/count histories are – some of them at least – group living animals.

According to the AHME book by Kery et al, “N-mixture models assume independence of detection, meaning individuals are detected independent from each other.” When we are dealing with animals occurring in groups, clearly we have the case where herds are easier to detect than solitary animals.


Remember, what we want from this analysis is to obtain three good models for the relative abundance of small/medium/large “species” of lion prey in the very large landscape, and – using spatial covariates – to generate predictive maps of lion prey availability in the entire landscape (even where we did not survey), so as to feed them as covariates in lion resource selection models.


So, is the group living natural history of our ungulates complicating our analysis to an extent that we should fall back to using Royle-Nichol models (and loose therefore the wealth of the count data that was painstakingly collected)?

Thank you very much for your suggestions. Searching the forum we did not find a similar discussion, and hopefully this question is of value to other people considering similar analysis (as more and more people try to “adapt” N-mixture models to their own research needs).


Thank you in advance.

Christos

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
parts:
Dear Christos,
 I would not recommend either of those models for modeling counts of grouped individuals.  You might consider doing a small simulation study to evaluate their performance for levels of aggregation that you have in your data. I'm guessing the results won't be so great but simulation might be a good way to better understand.
 The N-mixture and related models might work better for species that are not grouped -- but if you're counting tracks then you're potentially counting non-unique individuals. Modifications of the model could accommodate that but perhaps some development is required.
regards,
andy

messages.author: b03783d2b6589c68
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
parts:
Dear Andy,

First of all, thank you for taking the time to reply to the post. Discussing with the people who oversaw the data collection, we have a situation where skilled trackers counted fresh (day-old at most) tracks of ungulates crossing the sandy roads. As I understand it, the assumption violation of concern here is that antelope A that is part of a herd is likely more "visible/detectable" than antelope B that is moving alone and this means that the two antelopes differ in their detection probability. 

This difference in detectability would be (as I think about it) more of an issue if we were counting actual observed animals than tracks. Indeed, a herd of impala would attract ones attention and be spotted more often than a solitary impala. However, our trackers were moving along the road and had plenty of time (and tracking skills) to detect both solitary and herd moving animals as their tracks on sand are clear. Would the "herdiness" (grouping) of some tracks really make them more "detectable"? I see how one could make a point that this would not be the case. I am not asking this to try and find a way to wiggle around model assumption violations, but rather to better understand whether tracks can be used in general with N-mixture models. Of course, even if this was the case, we are left with the possibility that some of the tracks are of non-unique animals, as you say - i.e. that we may have double counted tracks of the same animal in the same survey period (here a spatial replication --> survey road segment of 2 km length). 

Most importantly however, why would "falling back" to using Royle-Nichols models (occuRN) would be also non advisable here? We would be using binary detect/non-detect data from each segment. How is the group moving nature of the study animals a concern here? Apologies if I am missing the obvious.

Finally, Martin et al. (2011) ("Accounting for non-independent detection when estimating abundance of organisms with a Bayesian framework") which you co-authored, introduces a beta binomial model that introduces a correlation parameter for animals living in a group (manatees in that case). Is that the path that you would recommend we look into when you mentioned above "modifications of the model could accomodate that", or did I misunderstand that?

Thanks again! Always great to learn (even if via many trials and errors).

Christos + team

messages.author: b07af4174ebf173b
messages.subject: Re: N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
parts:
Hi Christos,

how did you go with this? I am also currently working my way through a similar problem where I am attempting to estimate the abundance of rabbits and individual detections cannot be considered independent. 

I notice that Kery and Royle 2015 applied hierarchical modelling in ecology book, chapter 6, page 225 says that if observations cannot be considered independent then a possible way forward might be the choice of a beta-binomial distribution for the observation process.

I am in the process of working out how to, or if you can, incorporate a beta-binomial distribution into n-mixture models. I'd be keen to hear how you overcame your problem of non-independence of observations?

Cheers,
Pat

messages.author: 6d1a5b082ca0b806
messages.subject: Re: N-mixture model suitability when dealing with group living animals?
parts:
Hell, Pat.  I am using a Bayesian N-mixture model with beta-binomial for analyzing monitoring data for a species of pupfish.  The pupfish exhibit some degree of aggregation and the beta-binomial model works much better than the binomial for my case.  I've attached a text file (sc2019_nmix1a.txt) with the model code for WinBUGS called from R, just in case you are interested.  By way of a little background, the data are counts from minnow traps from 80 sites, each sampled three times.  As you can see, I modeled latent abundance with some coviariates.  Hope this is of some help.
John
